title: Sequence Containers
relevance: Interviewers probe which sequence container you default to and why—cache locality, growth, and invalidation—not just big-O tables.

phases.goal: Establish what a sequence container is and name the five Standard Library options with their storage models.

must_hit.point: A sequence container stores elements in a definite linear order; position is part of the meaning, unlike associative containers where keys decide placement.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says linear order / predecessor-successor; contrasts with key-based associative placement.

must_hit.point: The five sequence containers are std::vector (one contiguous heap block), std::array (inline fixed buffer of size N), std::deque (map of fixed-size chunks), std::list (doubly-linked heap nodes), and std::forward_list (singly-linked heap nodes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all five with matching storage models from the summary table.

must_hit.point: Default choice is std::vector unless you have a measured reason not to; interviewers want cache-locality reasoning.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Reaches for vector by default and mentions contiguous / cache-friendly layout.

must_hit.point: In Python, list is a dynamic array (like std::vector) and collections.deque is a double-ended queue (like std::deque); C++ exposes them as distinct types for strict control of layout and performance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps Python list→vector and deque→deque and notes C++’s stricter control.

probes: Which sequence container do you reach for by default, and why?
What distinguishes a sequence container from an associative container?

hints.1: Think about linear order versus key-based placement.
hints.2: Name the five containers and how each stores elements in memory.
hints.3: Default to std::vector for contiguous cache-friendly storage unless you have a measured reason otherwise.

phases.goal: Explain growth, access, and invalidation mechanics for vector, array, deque, list, and forward_list.

must_hit.point: vector tracks size (live elements) and capacity (allocated slots); reserve grows the buffer without changing size, while resize changes logical size by constructing or destroying elements.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates size vs capacity and contrasts reserve (no new elements) with resize (construct/destroy).

must_hit.point: To keep amortised O(1) push_back, vector grows geometrically (typically ~2× or ~1.5×); reallocation move/copies elements and invalidates all iterators, pointers, and references.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States geometric growth, amortised O(1), and full invalidation on realloc.

must_hit.point: Without realloc, vector insert/erase invalidates from the modification point to the end; pop_back invalidates only the removed last element.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the from-point-to-end and pop_back-only rules when capacity is not exceeded.

must_hit.point: std::array has compile-time size N as part of the type, inline storage (no heap), and no push_back/insert/reserve/resize growth API.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions N in the type, stack/embedded storage, and missing growth modifiers.

must_hit.point: deque is a map of fixed-size chunks: amortised O(1) push/pop at both ends and O(1) random access, but no reserve/capacity/data() and not one contiguous block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes chunk map, both-end O(1), indexing, and absence of contiguous/data/capacity.

must_hit.point: On deque, end insertions may invalidate all iterators while element pointers/references typically remain valid; middle insert/erase can invalidate iterators and references.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates iterator fragility from pointer/reference survival on end ops.

must_hit.point: list insert/erase is O(1) given an iterator (no operator[]); splice transfers nodes without copying; member sort is O(n log n) via pointer relinks because std::sort needs random access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers iterator-given O(1) edit, splice node transfer, and why list::sort exists.

must_hit.point: forward_list has no size(); edits use before_begin and insert_after/erase_after because nodes have only a next pointer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions missing size, before_begin, and after-oriented API for singly-linked nodes.

probes: What is the difference between reserve and resize on a vector?
How can deque offer O(1) push_front and random access?
Why does std::list have its own sort()?

hints.1: Separate logical size from allocated slots, and think about where each container puts memory.
hints.2: Walk vector reallocation, deque’s chunk map, list’s node rewiring, and forward_list’s predecessor iterators.
hints.3: reserve does not create elements; geometric growth invalidates everything on realloc; deque end-insert can keep references while killing iterators; list/forward_list only invalidate erased nodes.

phases.goal: Choose among vector, array, deque, list, and forward_list based on access pattern, ends vs middle, and cache cost.

must_hit.point: Even when list middle insert is O(1) and vector is O(n), contiguous vector often wins in practice due to cache lines versus list pointer chasing, until n is huge and you already hold a stable iterator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defaults to vector and cites cache locality / pointer chasing over raw big-O.

must_hit.point: Prefer deque for heavy push/pop at both ends plus indexing, or when vector realloc latency spikes are unacceptable; prefer array for fixed compile-time N with no heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Matches deque to both-end + index needs and array to fixed N / no heap.

must_hit.point: Prefer list for stable iterators, O(1) splice, or middle edit with an iterator already in hand; prefer forward_list for minimal node overhead and forward-only algorithms.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names iterator stability/splice for list and minimal singly-linked footprint for forward_list.

must_hit.point: For a binary buffer needing T* for C APIs, use vector or array data(); never deque or list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Requires contiguous data() and rejects deque/list for T* APIs.

probes: std::vector vs std::list—when is list actually justified?
When would you pick deque over vector?
std::array vs C array vs std::vector?

hints.1: Start from the access and insert/erase pattern you need.
hints.2: Map needs to default sequential, fixed N, both ends + index, stable splice, or minimal forward-only nodes.
hints.3: Default vector; array for fixed N/no heap; deque for both ends + indexing; list only for stability/splice with a known iterator; forward_list for minimal forward-only nodes.

phases.goal: Apply container rules to classic interview traps and justify a concrete choice under constraints.

must_hit.point: v[i] after reserve but before the element exists is undefined behaviour—reserve does not create elements.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that indexing reserved-but-unconstructed slots is UB.

must_hit.point: std::vector<bool> is a space-optimised specialisation returning a proxy from operator[]; you cannot bind bool&, take &v[i] as a real bool*, or assume contiguous bool storage—prefer vector<char>, deque<bool>, or a bitset.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names proxy reference, broken addressability, and safer alternatives.

must_hit.point: front(), back(), or pop_back() on an empty vector is undefined behaviour—check empty() first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags empty-container end access / pop as UB.

must_hit.point: list::unique only removes consecutive duplicates—sort first for global uniqueness; splice keeps iterators to transferred elements valid in the destination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions consecutive-only unique and splice iterator validity across lists.

probes: Explain amortised push_back and what reallocation invalidates.
You need queue-like push/pop at both ends and still want operator[]—what do you use?

hints.1: Watch for operations that look safe but do not create or relocate elements the way you expect.
hints.2: Tie the trap to storage model: packed bits, unconstructed capacity, or empty ends.
hints.3: vector<bool> returns a proxy; reserve ≠ construct; empty front/back/pop_back is UB; use deque for both-end + index.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Default to vector: contiguous scans beat list pointer chasing on modern CPUs even when big-O favors list insert, unless the container is massive and you already hold a stable iterator, or you need O(1) splice / iterator stability.

Use deque when you need push/pop at both ends with indexing, or when vector reallocations cause unacceptable latency spikes; vector remains better for single-block contiguous data() and simpler iterators.

tradeoffs.topic: std::array vs C array vs std::vector
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Fixed compile-time size and no heap → array (STL size/at/iterators, no pointer decay). Runtime size/growth → vector. Raw C arrays decay to pointers and do not carry size.

list for bidirectional edit, splice, and member algorithms with prev/next. forward_list when absolute minimum node size and forward-only passes matter, accepting before_begin / *_after APIs and no size().

gotchas.trap: Indexing or assuming elements exist after reserve
gotchas.correction: reserve only grows capacity; size is unchanged and new slots are uninitialised—creating elements requires resize, push_back/emplace_back, insert, or construction.

gotchas.trap: Assuming iterators stay valid across vector growth
gotchas.correction: Any op that may exceed capacity (push_back, insert, resize, reserve larger) can reallocate and invalidate all iterators, pointers, and references.

gotchas.trap: Treating deque iterators like pointers after end insert
gotchas.correction: End insertions may keep element pointers/references valid while invalidating iterators—do not assume pointer validity implies iterator validity; store indices or re-get iterators.

gotchas.trap: Using std::vector<bool> as a normal container of bool
gotchas.correction: It is a bit-packed specialisation: operator[] returns a proxy, not bool&; address-of and contiguous-bool assumptions fail—prefer vector<char>, deque<bool>, or a bitset.

gotchas.trap: Calling front/back/pop_back on an empty vector
gotchas.correction: Undefined behaviour—check empty() first in defensive code.

gotchas.trap: Expecting list::unique to remove all duplicates
gotchas.correction: unique only erases consecutive duplicates; for global uniqueness do sort then unique.

gotchas.trap: Trying to erase *it directly on forward_list
gotchas.correction: There is no erase(it) for the current node—keep the predecessor and call erase_after(pred); losing the previous iterator means restarting from before_begin().
